chapter_theme: The middle run of Pattinathar's general (பொது) verses: the body is a stinking frame that fire, worms, earth, kites, jackals and dogs each call their own, that mother, wives and sons abandon at the pyre, and that lust for women, whose every part stinks, keeps the mind bound to. Against it the poet sets the beggar's wealth (a loincloth, a bowl, the outer verandah, the five letters, holy ash), the renunciant who lives like a ghost and a corpse and a child, and a worship that has no drawn chakra, no spoken mantra, no built lingam, taught by the guru.
structure_note: The verses are addressed by turns to the body (354, 364, 375), to the poet's own heart (361, 365, 368, 370, 373), to the Lord (356, 366, 377) and to the townsfolk (367). Lists are the chapter's form: what claims the corpse (354), what the beggar owns (357, 360), what stinks (359), what the renunciant resembles (363), what the ritualist does (372), what the body is not for (377), what inner worship lacks (378). Several verses close on the refrain உனைப்போல் இல்லை பித்தரும் / பித்தனும் (361, and 388 in the next chapter).

354.reading: Fire says 'it is mine', the worm says 'mine', this earth says 'mine', the kite says 'mine, to eat', the jackal says 'mine', the base dog says 'mine': this stinking body I reared with love, and what gain do I have from it?
354.nuance: The six claimants are the six ends of a corpse: cremation, decay, burial, and the scavengers of the burning ground. The verse's bite is in பிரியமுடன் வளர்த்தேன், that the poet fed with love what was never his but already spoken for.

355.reading: This town where the Lord's street is the king's seat, where the ornamented soldiers and the command of the thirty-six (four nines) reach, with its kitchen comfort for sudden hunger: countless ages we have let it go to waste, past counting.
355.nuance: The verse reads as cipher: இவ்வூர், this town, is taken by tradition as the body, with the Lord's street its central channel and நாலொன்பது, four nines, the thirty-six tattvas as the soldiers who serve it. A plain reading, a real town with a royal street, garrison and alms-kitchen wasted for ages, is possible but makes the number idle. The last line, that incalculable time has been lost, is the same on either reading.

356.reading: The mothers who bore me reviled me as a corpse and left; the wives who got my gold said 'go' and wailed and left; the sons I got went round behind me and broke the pot; so, Lord, apart from clinging to you there is no clinging at all.
356.nuance: குடம் உடைத்தல் is the funeral rite in which the son circles the pyre and breaks the water pot, the last act of kinship. The three lines run through the three bonds of a man's life and end each at the burning ground; the conclusion is not grief but a transfer of attachment to the one party who does not leave.

357.reading: Unstained teeth, a loincloth of rag, a heart patient and without guile, poor food, the outer verandah, sleeping on the ground and the bowl one begs with: the great Veda calls out, so the world may know, that this is wealth without lack.
357.nuance: கறையற்ற பல் may be teeth unstained by betel, a mark of the man who has given up the householder's pleasures, or simply clean. The claim that the Veda itself proclaims this is the poet's authority for inverting wealth; the list is of things anyone could have, so the wealth is in wanting nothing more.

358.reading: The light that stands as one in the eight directions and sixteen corners, everywhere, surging and sprouting and rising high: fools all bind it and roll it up and keep it under their arm, and do not keep it in thought; they are the wrongdoers who call broad day night.
358.nuance: கட்டிச் சுருட்டித் தங்கக் கக்கத்தில் வைப்பர் is the gesture of tying up palm-leaf books and carrying them under the arm, so the fools are the learned who hold the all-pervading light as a text and not in the heart. எட்டுத் திசையும் பதினாறு கோணமும் may be a plain figure for everywhere or a yantra's eight directions and sixteen petals; the sense does not turn on it.

359.reading: The mouth stinks of spittle, the knotted hair stinks, the kohl-painted eyes stink, the body stinks of excrement, the great pit of the mouth stinks like a burst corpse, the yoni stinks of pus, the mud of the senses stinks and spills: how did the mind cling to women like this?
359.nuance: A catalogue of disgust in the manner of the Naladiyar's body verses, aimed not at women as such but at the mind that chose them (மனம் பற்றியதே). The word நாறும் is repeated seven times; the verse argues by smell alone.

360.reading: I have the good five holy letters to say, and say them as told; I have holy ash to wear with pride; from the street rubbish heap I have a rag to wear as a loincloth; I have resolved to beg from any caste: there is nothing I lack.
360.nuance: எந்தச் சாதியிலும் இரக்க, to beg from any caste, is the renunciant's indifference to who gives the food, and so a quiet refusal of caste rules on eating. The verse answers 357: the same inventory, now in the first person.

361.reading: You have suffered, and still you have not come to know, 'this is what will befall me next'; you have not gone to the good; with petty understanding you were tormented; in the bewitchment of young women's arts you were made a fool, O heart; there is no madman like you.
361.nuance: மடமானார் கல்வி மயக்கம் is read here as the spell cast by women's accomplishments; it could also be the delusion of learning in general, with மடமானார் as a separate object of torment. பாடு in line 1 is what one undergoes, so படும் பாட்டை is the coming suffering, not a song.

362.reading: Free of craving, free of hard deeds, free of kin and of occupations, free of the hidden hand-holding of women, free of worry, praising with a full mouth the Lord who comes, the mind subdued and no spreading out: is that not, Supreme One, supreme bliss?
362.nuance: The verse defines bliss by subtraction, six அற்று (free of) in a row, before the one positive act of praise. பரப்பற்று, without spreading, is the mind not reaching outward; the whole is a description of the renunciant's state rather than an instruction.

363.reading: They wander like ghosts, lie like corpses, eat whatever alms are given like dogs, roam like jackals, regard good women as their mother, speak humbly to everyone as to kin, and stay like children: see, these are the ones clear in true knowledge.
363.nuance: The seven comparisons are to what the world despises (ghost, corpse, dog, jackal) and to what it protects (mother, kin, child); the jnani is placed outside honour on both sides. The verse is a portrait of the poet's own way of life, as 357 and 360 are.

364.reading: Prey for kites, feast for vultures, twist made by the vain one with the water pot, dwelling where worms come to stay, carcass without any good, bondage that even the mother who bore it will not touch once the instruments go slack: I have carried you, and what pleasure is there in you for me?
364.nuance: கமண்டல வீணன் is Brahma with his water pot, called a wastrel for making this body; முடக்கு, a bend or twist, is the crooked thing he made. கருவி, the instruments, are the senses and organs; when they fail the body becomes untouchable even to its mother. Addressed to the body, as 354 and 375 are.

365.reading: What use is weeping, what use is grieving, it does not help; what use is worshipping; what use is the harm of someone speaking to burn you; will good and evil come otherwise than as the lotus-born one wrote? Do not be shaken, my poor heart.
365.nuance: The verse puts worship (தொழுதல்) in the same list as weeping and grief, as things that cannot change what Brahma has written. This is a counsel of steadiness, not of fatalism as a doctrine: its point is சலியாதிரு, do not waver, and the fate argument is the reason given.

366.reading: Not following the rich and talking them up and showing my teeth every day in anguish, let me enter within the bounds of supreme bliss, rightly solitary, and stay free of trouble in the place that is mine, O rare substance in the banyan's shade.
366.nuance: ஆலநீழல் அரும்பொருள் is Dakshinamurti, the silent teacher under the banyan, the fitting addressee for a prayer to be left alone. பல்லினைக் காட்டி, baring the teeth, is the forced smile of the dependent; the verse refuses patronage, not wealth as such.

367.reading: Townsfolk, hear a teaching for you: smear over your whole body the ash that sent the Jains to the stake, lie on the outer verandah, leave the tangle of kin and let the world laugh; the Lord himself will give you his twin feet.
367.nuance: சமணைக் கழுவேற்று நீறு is the holy ash of Sambandar's Madurai contest, after which the Jains were impaled, so the ash is named by its victory. The teaching is the poet's own practice (357, 360) offered to the town, with ridicule (சக நகைக்க) counted as part of the method.

368.reading: What is it to put on ash, what is it to go and bathe, my heart, when you have not learned the way to be born differently; what did you see of the seven crore mantras loaded in the great Veda-book; lying in the river, you drift without knowing the ford.
368.nuance: மாற்றிப் பிறக்க வகை, the way to change one's birth, is the thing the rites and the Veda have not given; ஆற்றிற் கிடந்தும் துறை அறியாமல் makes the river both the bathing place and the river of birth. The verse does not reject ash and bathing, it says they are no use without the knowing.

369.reading: If one knows the fruit of the single seed that came and sprouted rightly in the drop that stood as Om, then the fourteen worlds, without leaving, leave; one fills the unfilled and becomes the filled form; and for those who were ego, the Eight-fold one comes near and stays.
369.nuance: The verse is cipher throughout. ஓங்காரமாய் நின்ற அந்து (bindu) and the seed sprouting in it is the manifestation of the world from Om and bindu, as tradition reads it, or the forming of the body from the drop in the womb; both are Siddhar readings and the poet may intend both. எட்டர் is taken as Siva of the eight forms (அட்டமூர்த்தி); ஆங்காரமானவர்க்கு, for those who were ahankara, is read as 'even for the egoists', though it may be those who have become the I-sound. The sense turns on these terms and the reading given is a tradition, not the verse's plain statement.

370.reading: Brahma's creating, Vishnu's protecting and the hurling (of destruction) by the lord of wide Kailasa will not come near us; take supreme bliss as your goal, hold all the rest as a dream in sleep and do not regard it, my heart; see, this is good medicine for you.
370.nuance: தொடைப்பு is hard; it may be the Kailasa lord's act of throwing down, i.e. destruction, completing the three gods' three acts, or a corruption. The claim is that one who takes bliss as the goal is outside the whole cycle of creation and dissolution; the dream figure makes the world unreal only relative to that.

371.reading: The dog has the stick and we have alms; to defeat Death we have the five-letter mantra in the mouth; for ghosts that come without regard we have ash; for the bewildered disease of birth we have the gracious look of the teacher's eye.
371.nuance: A verse of remedies, each உண்டு (there is) matched to a threat. The first line is self-mocking: what the beggar gets at the door is placed beside what the dog gets. The last, the guru's glance (அருள் நோக்கம்) curing the disease of rebirth, is the Saiva teaching of initiation by sight.

372.reading: Observances, vows, the Vedas, the Agamas, the way of right conduct, fire rites, water offerings, the twilight prayers, japa, mantra, the states of yoga, the names, sandal and holy ash put on with care, and the pujas these people do at every watch of the day: all of it is pretence.
372.nuance: சர்ப்பனை is read as சற்பனை, fabrication, so the whole list is false show. The list is wide enough to include யோக நிலை and the five names, which the poet elsewhere prizes (360, 371); the attack may fall on these people (இவர் செய்யும்) rather than on the practices. Whether the verse condemns the rites or their performers is open.

373.reading: However much sense I talked, you did not listen, good heart; why do you go astray like this and ruin yourself; like one who casts a strong hook for the fish in the sky where nothing is, you think of getting back what is gone: what sense is this?
373.nuance: வானத்தின் மீன், the fish in the sky, is a star (மீன் means both), so the hook thrown at it is desire for what cannot be reached. போனத்தை மீள நினைத்தல், wanting back what has passed, may be lost wealth, youth or past pleasures; the verse does not say.

374.reading: With the axe called the five letters I cut out at the root the stump of the five senses, the deceiving field of sense; I tilled and improved the ground, planted the knowledge called Sadasiva, pulled the weeds of the crowd, and raised the crop of Siva's enjoyment.
374.nuance: An extended farming figure: clearing, tilling, sowing, weeding, harvest. புஞ்சக் களை may be the weeds of the senses' crowd or the dry-land weeds; either way they are what grows back after the stump is cut. சிவபோகம், Siva-enjoyment, is the harvest, so the verse ends in bliss, not in bare renunciation.

375.reading: On the day you sink and mother, kin and wife cast you off and say 'who are you, who am I', at that very moment diseases come and settle in; and besides the disease you have taken on and a mat, what friend have you, O body?
375.nuance: நீயார் நானார், 'who are you, who am I', is the formula of disowning. The friends left at the end are a disease and a mat: the verse is addressed to the body and tells it that its own company deserts it before death, not only after.

376.reading: Look closely: in every hair-pore worms crowd and soak; when the body that has become a dung pit is burned, even the ghosts dance there, people say; did you not know this, and yet you thought of hunting wealth?
376.nuance: கடம் ஆம் is read as the body becoming a (burning) ground where ghosts dance; the line may instead say the body is a pot (கடம்). The argument is that seeking wealth for a body of this kind is the folly, not wealth itself.

377.reading: Not fit to wear as ornament, not for gold, not for seeing the earth, not for women, not for good sights, not for the feet of Siva who is beyond the far: with my thought ruined, the trouble this servant takes to rear a span of body is not small.
377.nuance: The body is weighed against every use, worldly and divine, and found fit for none, the last (சிவனடிக்கு அல்ல) being the surprise: even for the Lord's feet it is no instrument. சாண், a span, is the body's measure of contempt.

378.reading: A chakra not drawn, a mantra not spoken, a flower no one else can reach, holy water that does not run dry, a lingam not built once this is ended, a heart that does not think: puja that does not fail, within the thought itself: is that not what the guru taught?
378.nuance: Each item of outer worship (yantra, mantra, flower, water, lingam) is named by what it is not, so the puja is wholly inward; கருதாத நெஞ்சம், the heart that does not think, makes even the inner act an absence. இனிமுடிந்து is hard to place: 'henceforth, finished' or 'once this body ends'. The authority claimed is the guru's word, not the poet's own.

links.note: Both make the body food for the scavengers before it is dead: Arunagirinathar's mass of filth and worms is food for jackals, vultures and crows and stinks the moment life leaves; Pattinathar's fire, worm, earth, kite, jackal and dog each already call it theirs. Both end on the folly of having cherished it.

The same roll of claimants on the body: here fire, worm, earth, kite, jackal and dog say 'mine'; at 428 dogs, jackals, ghosts and vultures hold the fat belly to be theirs while 'we' call it ours. 428 turns the image into a reason not to harm anyone.

Both follow the loving ones to the moment they leave: Tirumular's storehouse loses its fastenings, the nine gates shut and the loving ones wept and went; Pattinathar's mother calls him a corpse, the wives say 'go' and the sons break the pot. Pattinathar adds the conclusion, that the only attachment left is to the Lord.

Pattinathar calls the begging bowl, the loincloth and the verandah wealth without lack, proclaimed by the Veda; the Kural says that if one must live by begging, let the world's maker wander and perish. On the Kural's plain reading begging is the worst of lives; for Pattinathar it is the chosen one. The conflict holds unless the Kural is read as about the poor who beg from need rather than the renunciant.

Tirumular allows that the true garb receives alms but adds that a garb saves only those who have understood; Pattinathar's list of the beggar's goods makes no such condition. 363 supplies it from the poet's side, the beggar's way being that of those clear in true knowledge.

Both set the bundled book against the Lord: Sivavakkiyar's shastras recited and books tied in bundles ended as nothing once he knew the Lord; Pattinathar's fools roll up the all-pervading light and carry it under the arm instead of keeping it in thought.

Both poets use deliberately foul anatomy of the woman's body to break desire: Arunagirinathar's well, channel of old stains and rotting hole; Pattinathar's seven stenches ending at the yoni and the mud of the senses. Both close by turning on the poet's own mind that clung.

Sivavakkiyar argues that caste has no substance, since all bodies are the same five elements through the same gate; Pattinathar does not argue but acts, resolving to beg from any caste as part of lacking nothing. The doctrine of one becomes the practice of the other.

Tirumular's Siva-gnanis wander as men dead while their senses and body remain intact; Pattinathar's knowers of true jnana wander like ghosts and lie like corpses. Both describe the jnani by his resemblance to the dead and set him against other kinds of ascetic or ritualist.

Pattinathar tells the heart that good and evil come only as Brahma wrote, so that even worship changes nothing and the right stance is not to waver; the Kural says those who toil without flagging will see fate's back. On Pattinathar's plain reading, no effort alters the outcome; the Kural claims effort can. The tension softens only if 365 is read as counsel for the mind's peace rather than a claim about causation.

Tirumular lists what becomes needless once the Life of life is within (recitation, desire, dying, going about); Pattinathar lists the vows, Vedas, Agamas, fire rites, japa and pujas and calls them pretence. Tirumular's list is of things outgrown, Pattinathar's of things false, but both set the whole ritual apparatus aside.

Tirumular makes the heart the temple, the body the shrine, the soul the lingam and the senses the lamps, so that worship is translated into the body; Pattinathar goes further and names each outer item by its absence, a chakra not drawn, a lingam not built, a heart that does not think. Tirumular's inner temple is still furnished; Pattinathar's inner puja has nothing in it.

Sivavakkiyar asks what mantra it is to circle a planted stone and mutter while the Lord is within; Pattinathar answers with the worship the guru taught, which has no planted lingam and no spoken mantra. Both rest on the Lord being within the worshipper.

source_issues: 370 line 2 தொடைப்பு is doubtful; the expected third act of the three gods (destruction) is not clearly named.
376 line 3 பேயும் நடனமிடுங் கடமாம் is obscure; கடம் may be a corrupt word.
378 line 2 இனிமுடிந்து sits awkwardly between the water and the lingam and may belong to another line.
